Financial translation: why your business needs a specialist

November 14, 2023
Business | Communication

Financial documents move money, and they carry legal weight. When one crosses a language border, a small slip can change what a figure, a risk or an obligation means to the person reading it.

Financial translation is the translation of reports, statements, fund documents and investor communications by linguists who understand both the language and the accounting framework behind it. It is a different discipline from general business translation, and the gap shows first in the terminology.

Below you will find what a specialist adds, which documents need one and how to choose a provider. The examples use English and French, a pairing that matters for UK firms trading with France, Belgium, Switzerland and Canada.

Benefits of a specialised financial translation service

A specialist protects the meaning of your numbers, your terminology and your regulatory position. The benefits fall into four areas.

Accurate terminology

Finance has its own vocabulary, and many terms change meaning between countries. In UK English, “stock” normally means inventories, while in US English it usually means shares. A translator who does not know which framework the document follows can choose the wrong French or German term and leave the reader with a different balance sheet.

Accounting concepts matter just as much. Accruals sit among liabilities, while prepayments are assets, so a translator needs to recognise both at a glance.

The right accounting framework

UK groups that are listed apply UK-adopted international accounting standards, and many other UK companies report under UK GAAP such as FRS 102, which the Financial Reporting Council issues. French companies report under the Plan comptable général (PCG). Some measures have no exact counterpart: French reporting uses EBE (excédent brut d’exploitation), which is close to EBITDA but defined differently, so the translator has to check how each figure is calculated before choosing a term.

Regulatory fit

If your firm is regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority, a financial promotion must be fair, clear and not misleading under COBS 4.2.1R, and a translated version has to meet the same standard as the English original. Filing rules apply too. Companies House requires accounts prepared in another language to be accompanied by a certified translation into English.

Fewer corrections later

A weak translation of a report or memorandum usually comes back as a query from a lender, an auditor or a regulator. A specialist translator, working with a glossary and a second-linguist check, catches those problems before the document leaves your desk.

Financial documents that need translation

These are typical financial documents, and each one carries real consequences if the translation is wrong.

  • Key investor information documents (KIID)
  • Investment fund reports
  • Investor reports and investor relations materials
  • Balance sheets
  • Income statements
  • Financial reporting guidelines
  • Bank documents
  • Information memorandums
  • Due diligence papers
  • Risk management and asset management documents
  • Audit reports

Investor reports and fund documents also have an editorial dimension. They speak to readers with different expectations, so a translator has to adapt tone and structure as well as vocabulary. Asset managers marketing funds abroad should treat translation as part of the compliance process rather than a final formatting step.

Financial interpreting for meetings and results calls

Documents are only half of cross-border finance. Board meetings, investor presentations, due diligence sessions and results calls all need clear spoken communication as well.

An interpreter with financial experience handles the numbers and the vocabulary live, and a briefing pack beforehand lets them prepare. For virtual meetings, remote interpreting avoids travel and works across time zones.

Choosing a financial translation provider

Look for evidence of financial specialisation, not just a long list of languages. Ask who will translate your files, what qualifications or sector experience they hold and whether they translate into their native language.

Ask about process too. A provider should maintain a terminology base for your company, follow your preferred style and include proofreading by a second linguist. Clear communication matters as much as the translation itself, because questions about a figure need answers before delivery, not after.

Working with the same team over time pays off. They learn how your firm describes its products and results, and your documents stay consistent from one reporting period to the next, whether you work in French, German, Spanish or another language.

Frequently asked questions

What is financial translation?

Financial translation is the specialist translation of documents such as annual reports, fund factsheets, investor presentations and bank paperwork. The translator needs to know the accounting framework, the regulatory context and the terminology of both languages.

Do I need a certified translation of my accounts?

For Companies House, accounts prepared in another language must be filed with a certified English translation. Other bodies, such as banks, regulators and courts, set their own requirements, so check with the recipient before you commission the work.

Can a bilingual accountant translate financial reports?

Fluency alone is not enough. Translation is a separate skill from accounting, and a bilingual accountant may not know the target-language reporting conventions or have a second reader to check the result.

Which languages can you handle for financial translation?

BeTranslated covers financial work in French, German, Spanish, Korean and many other languages. The right linguist depends on the document type, the target market and the reporting framework involved.

Do you offer financial interpreting as well as translation?

Yes. Interpreters with financial experience cover board meetings, investor calls and due diligence sessions, in person or remotely. Tell us the subject and the participants, and we will match a suitable linguist.
